question: Is a clock worth its price only in a world with rhythm? A crystal clock (q5-bound's, near the TUR bound) anticipates the next event of a world whose intervals are gamma-distributed with mean T = 20 and shape k from 1 (Poisson: no memory) to periodic. How much does a clock 64 times dearer anticipate better, by world?
seeds: seed(name) = int(sha256('<registration id>:<beacon randomness>:<name>').hexdigest()[:12], 16): a clock's crystal from its name, a world's events from 'world:<world name>' (the same events for every clock); numpy PCG64.
beacon: drand quicknet (chain 52db9ba70e0cc0f6eaf7803dd07447a1f5477735fd3f661792ba94600c84e971): the first round dated at or after the earliest GitHub-witnessed push (GET repos/s0fractal/time-lab/activity) that holds the commit adding q6-renewal/registration.lock.json.

design.readout: the agent stores Φ at each event; at each query (every query_every from warm to t_total) it reads â = (Φ(now) − Φ(last event)) / v* and predicts the time to the next event as m_k(â) = E[τ − a | τ > a] at a = â for gamma(k, T / k) intervals (periodic: max(T − â, 0)); perfect reads the true a; none predicts T (1 + 1/k) / 2. Events fall on the sub-step grid, from a uniform offset in [0, T).

hypotheses.statement: An irregular world caps what precision is worth: in a world of shape 16 (interval sd T/4), the clock of 64 phases, which costs 64 times the entropy of the clock of 1, anticipates the next event less than 10% better.
hypotheses.rule: For each clock, of its mean phase Φ = J / (N d) at the checkpoints (400, 800, 1800), 1024 trajectories: D = [var(Φ(t2) − Φ(t0)) − var(Φ(t1) − Φ(t0))] / (2 (t2 − t1)), v = mean(Φ(t2) − Φ(t0)) / (t2 − t0), S = the mean heat given to the bath over [t0, t2] / (σ² (t2 − t0)). For each clock and world, over every query of every trajectory: MSE = the mean squared error of the predicted time to the next event, m_k(â) with â = (Φ(now) − Φ(last event)) / v*; MSE(none) predicts the mean residual life T (1 + 1/k) / 2 (T / 2 periodic); MSE(perfect) reads the true elapsed time. Each test is log10 of a ratio, with a 95% interval (inverted-cdf quantiles) over 2000 resamples of the trajectories, the same indices for every clock and world, seeded from the registration id; any resample in which the ratio is undefined makes the hypothesis inconclusive. Supported if the interval of log10 MSE(N1) / MSE(N64) in the world k16 lies below log10 1.1; contradicted if it lies wholly above; else inconclusive.

hypotheses.statement: A periodic world sells anticipation at the entropy price: the clock of 64 phases anticipates better than the clock of 1 by the ratio of their entropy rates, within ×1.25 either way.
hypotheses.rule: For each clock, of its mean phase Φ = J / (N d) at the checkpoints (400, 800, 1800), 1024 trajectories: D = [var(Φ(t2) − Φ(t0)) − var(Φ(t1) − Φ(t0))] / (2 (t2 − t1)), v = mean(Φ(t2) − Φ(t0)) / (t2 − t0), S = the mean heat given to the bath over [t0, t2] / (σ² (t2 − t0)). For each clock and world, over every query of every trajectory: MSE = the mean squared error of the predicted time to the next event, m_k(â) with â = (Φ(now) − Φ(last event)) / v*; MSE(none) predicts the mean residual life T (1 + 1/k) / 2 (T / 2 periodic); MSE(perfect) reads the true elapsed time. Each test is log10 of a ratio, with a 95% interval (inverted-cdf quantiles) over 2000 resamples of the trajectories, the same indices for every clock and world, seeded from the registration id; any resample in which the ratio is undefined makes the hypothesis inconclusive. Supported if the interval of log10 [MSE(N1) / MSE(N64)] − log10 [S(N64) / S(N1)] in the periodic world lies within (−log10 1.25, log10 1.25); contradicted if it lies wholly outside; else inconclusive.

hypotheses.statement: Even a regular world caps it: in a world of shape 4096 (interval sd T/64), 64 times the entropy anticipates less than four times better.
hypotheses.rule: For each clock, of its mean phase Φ = J / (N d) at the checkpoints (400, 800, 1800), 1024 trajectories: D = [var(Φ(t2) − Φ(t0)) − var(Φ(t1) − Φ(t0))] / (2 (t2 − t1)), v = mean(Φ(t2) − Φ(t0)) / (t2 − t0), S = the mean heat given to the bath over [t0, t2] / (σ² (t2 − t0)). For each clock and world, over every query of every trajectory: MSE = the mean squared error of the predicted time to the next event, m_k(â) with â = (Φ(now) − Φ(last event)) / v*; MSE(none) predicts the mean residual life T (1 + 1/k) / 2 (T / 2 periodic); MSE(perfect) reads the true elapsed time. Each test is log10 of a ratio, with a 95% interval (inverted-cdf quantiles) over 2000 resamples of the trajectories, the same indices for every clock and world, seeded from the registration id; any resample in which the ratio is undefined makes the hypothesis inconclusive. Supported if the interval of log10 MSE(N1) / MSE(N64) in the world k4096 lies below log10 4; contradicted if it lies wholly above; else inconclusive.

hypotheses.statement: On a horizon of one interval the clock of 1 anticipates better than a Brownian clock of its own long-time diffusion would, in the periodic world (the expected reason: its velocity relaxes in 1/γ = 2, so its reading of an elapsed time a errs with variance 2 (D/v²)(a − (1 − e^(−γa))/γ), not 2 (D/v²) a).
hypotheses.rule: For each clock, of its mean phase Φ = J / (N d) at the checkpoints (400, 800, 1800), 1024 trajectories: D = [var(Φ(t2) − Φ(t0)) − var(Φ(t1) − Φ(t0))] / (2 (t2 − t1)), v = mean(Φ(t2) − Φ(t0)) / (t2 − t0), S = the mean heat given to the bath over [t0, t2] / (σ² (t2 − t0)). For each clock and world, over every query of every trajectory: MSE = the mean squared error of the predicted time to the next event, m_k(â) with â = (Φ(now) − Φ(last event)) / v*; MSE(none) predicts the mean residual life T (1 + 1/k) / 2 (T / 2 periodic); MSE(perfect) reads the true elapsed time. Each test is log10 of a ratio, with a 95% interval (inverted-cdf quantiles) over 2000 resamples of the trajectories, the same indices for every clock and world, seeded from the registration id; any resample in which the ratio is undefined makes the hypothesis inconclusive. In the periodic world the time to the next event is T − a, so a Brownian clock of the clock's own D and v errs with MSE_B = 2 (D / v²) mean(a), mean(a) over the same queries. Supported if the interval of log10 MSE_B(N1) / MSE(N1) in the periodic world lies above 0; contradicted if it lies wholly below; else inconclusive.

hypotheses.statement: What precision is worth grows in proportion to the world's regularity: a clock 16 times dearer in a world 16 times more regular gets the same share of what a perfect clock anticipates there (the clock of 16 in the world of shape 4096 against the clock of 1 in the world of shape 256), within ×1.1 either way.
hypotheses.rule: For each clock, of its mean phase Φ = J / (N d) at the checkpoints (400, 800, 1800), 1024 trajectories: D = [var(Φ(t2) − Φ(t0)) − var(Φ(t1) − Φ(t0))] / (2 (t2 − t1)), v = mean(Φ(t2) − Φ(t0)) / (t2 − t0), S = the mean heat given to the bath over [t0, t2] / (σ² (t2 − t0)). For each clock and world, over every query of every trajectory: MSE = the mean squared error of the predicted time to the next event, m_k(â) with â = (Φ(now) − Φ(last event)) / v*; MSE(none) predicts the mean residual life T (1 + 1/k) / 2 (T / 2 periodic); MSE(perfect) reads the true elapsed time. Each test is log10 of a ratio, with a 95% interval (inverted-cdf quantiles) over 2000 resamples of the trajectories, the same indices for every clock and world, seeded from the registration id; any resample in which the ratio is undefined makes the hypothesis inconclusive. The share of the ceiling is C = MSE(perfect) / MSE(clock) in a world. Supported if the interval of log10 C(N16 in k4096) / C(N1 in k256) lies within (−log10 1.1, log10 1.1); contradicted if it lies wholly outside; else inconclusive.
